content.title: About
content.content: Biscuit is a light, airy baked good made from flour, eggs, sugar and a small amount of fat. It is commonly served in fast‑food outlets and restaurants as a standalone dessert, a cake base, or as a sandwich with various fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Biscuit originated in Europe in the 19th century as a lighter alternative to traditional cakes.
Traditional biscuit contains no leavening agents; its fluffiness comes from whipped egg whites.
In some countries the biscuit is called “soft” because of its tender texture.
Biscuit is often used as a base for mille‑feuille and trifle desserts.
Both sweet and savory versions exist, served with sauces, fruit, or simply dusted with powdered sugar.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Biscuit usually contains less fat than many other baked goods, making it a lighter snack option.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: It provides a quick source of energy through simple carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the recipe add a modest amount of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Its airy structure allows rapid digestion, suitable for a light bite.

items.title: Can be fortified
items.content: Recipes often incorporate fruit purées or nuts, boosting vitamin and mineral content.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Biscuit is typically made with wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Sugar and simple carbs may cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, so those with diabetes should limit portions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional biscuits are often sweet, contributing to dental decay and weight gain when consumed excessively.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Store‑bought biscuits may contain additives and preservatives that are not suitable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Biscuit can be enjoyed on its own, sliced and served with berry sauce, used as a cake layer, made into sandwiches with ham, cheese or vegetables, or toasted for a crisp crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep biscuits in an airtight container at room temperature, away from direct light. For longer storage place them in the refrigerator, and for several months store them in the freezer. Before eating, check for any mold or off‑odors.
